The core challenge in human action recognition lies in temporal consistency—how to extract meaningful motion patterns from noisy visual streams. Temporal coherence maps provide a structured abstraction where pixel brightness changes are aggregated into motion events, forming a sparse yet informative representation. This aligns with event cameras' architecture, which emit asynchronous spikes based on intensity variation rather than fixed frame rates. These maps enable high-efficiency temporal processing at the hardware level, bypassing traditional convolutional approaches. Synthetic video generation addresses dataset bias by augmenting real-world data with diverse, conditionally generated sequences, effectively expanding the support of action manifolds. Reinforcement learning further reduces dependency on labeled data by optimizing policies directly from environmental rewards, leveraging intrinsic motivation and exploration strategies. Each primitive operates under distinct assumptions: event cameras assume temporal precision, synthetic generation assumes semantic fidelity, and RL assumes reward structure alignment. Failure modes include loss of temporal resolution in low-light conditions, poor generalization in synthetic domains, and policy collapse in sparse reward landscapes.
